title: Novartis ianalumab two-year data at ACR show further improvements in Sjögren’s disease activity
body_markdown:
- *Patients continuing ianalumab saw further improvement in systemic disease activity through Week 108, with no new safety findings* *1*


- *Nearly two-thirds of patients on continuous ianalumab reached low disease activity at Week 108* *1*


- *Improvements in stimulated salivary flow were maintained in patients with baseline salivary flow >0.4mL/min continuing ianalumab* *1*


- *Patients who switched from placebo to ianalumab monthly saw improvements across most efficacy outcomes, including an increase in low disease activity rates* *1*


**Basel, November 10, 2026** – Novartis today presented long-term results from the ongoing NEPTUNUS extension study of ianalumab in Sjögren’s disease at the American College of Rheumatology Convergence 2026. The data showed that the reduction in systemic disease activity continued to deepen from Week 48 through Week 108 among patients who continued ianalumab 300 mg monthly as measured by EULAR Sjögren’s Syndrome Disease Activity Index (ESSDAI).1


Improvements were also sustained in physician- and patient-reported outcomes as well as salivary flow.1 Additionally, most efficacy outcomes improved after patients switched from placebo to ianalumab.1 Adverse event and serious adverse event rates were comparable between the two treatment arms through Week 204, with no new safety findings.1


“Sjögren’s disease is chronic and systemic, requiring treatment options that can provide sustained disease control over the long term,” said Thomas Dörner, Department of Medicine and Clinical Immunology at Charité – Universitätsmedizin Berlin and Deutsches Rheuma-Forschungszentrum Berlin, ein Leibniz-Institut. “These data provide important new insights into long-term treatment response and deepen our understanding of the disease.”


**Key findings** ¹


- At Week 108, ESSDAI reductions continued to deepen with longer ianalumab treatment, with a mean reduction from core-study baseline of 7.5 points in the group that continued ianalumab monthly and 6.5 points in the group that switched from placebo to ianalumab monthly at Week 60.
- Low disease activity (LDA) rates increased from 57.1% to 65.1% in the continuous ianalumab monthly group between Weeks 48 and 108. In patients who switched from placebo to ianalumab monthly at Week 60, LDA rates increased from 50.4% to 60.9%.
- Among patients with stimulated salivary flow greater than 0.4 mL/min at baseline, improvements were maintained through Week 96 in the continuous ianalumab monthly group and observed after patients switched from placebo to ianalumab at Week 60.
- Improvements in physician- and patient-reported measures and symptoms were sustained through Week 108 among patients who continued ianalumab monthly, measured by ESSPRI and SSSD, and were observed following the switch from placebo to ianalumab at Week 60.


Sjögren’s disease is a serious, systemic autoimmune disease in which B-cell dysfunction plays a significant role, contributing to inflammation, tissue damage and symptoms including dryness, fatigue, pain and organ involvement, which can substantially impact patients’ daily lives.2-6 Targeted therapies are needed to address systemic disease activity, as there are no approved options currently available outside China.7


“These findings strengthen the growing body of evidence for ianalumab and reinforce our commitment to advancing a targeted treatment that can improve care for people living with Sjögren’s disease,” said Angelika Jahreis, Global Head, Development, Immunology, Novartis. “The novel dual mechanism of ianalumab is designed to target B-cell dysfunction, which plays a significant role in this complex disease.”


Ianalumab is currently under review by regulatory authorities in multiple countries, including the US where a decision from the Food and Drug Administration is expected this year. The NEPTUNUS-1 and NEPTUNUS-2 studies were the first global Phase III trials to demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in Sjögren’s disease activity.8,9,10 The NEPTUNUS extension study is ongoing to continue evaluating the longer-term efficacy, safety and tolerability of ianalumab.1,11


**About ianalumab**
Ianalumab is a fully human monoclonal antibody with a novel dual mechanism of action that depletes B cells and inhibits their activation and survival via BAFF-R blockade.12 Novartis is investigating ianalumab for its ability to treat B-cell driven diseases, including Sjögren’s disease, immune thrombocytopenia (ITP), systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), lupus nephritis (LN), and systemic sclerosis (SSc).9-11,13-16


**About the NEPTUNUS program**
NEPTUNUS-1 and NEPTUNUS-2 are global, multicenter, pivotal Phase III trials evaluating the efficacy and safety of ianalumab in people with Sjögren’s disease.9,10 NEPTUNUS-1 evaluated ianalumab 300 mg subcutaneously (s.c.) monthly versus placebo for 52 weeks, while NEPTUNUS-2 evaluated ianalumab 300 mg s.c. monthly or every three months versus placebo for up to 52 weeks.9,10 The primary endpoint in both trials assessed improvement in systemic disease activity using ESSDAI. Participants completing the core studies were eligible to enter an ongoing NEPTUNUS extension trial evaluating the long-term efficacy, safety and tolerability of ianalumab.11 The interim analysis of the extension trial includes patients who continued ianalumab and patients who switched from placebo to ianalumab at Week 60.1


**About Sjögren’s disease**
Sjögren’s disease is a complex, systemic autoimmune disease that causes inflammation and tissue damage, impacting the entire body.5 It primarily affects exocrine glands, leading to excessive dryness, with over 90% of patients experiencing dry eyes and dry mouth.5,6 The disease is heterogenous and inflicts a wide range of symptoms, with patients most commonly experiencing dryness, fatigue and widespread pain, though 30-40% of patients will also show extraglandular organ involvement.17,18 The risk of lymphoma is increased in patients with Sjögren’s.17 Sjögren’s affects approximately 0.25% of the population with an estimated 50% undiagnosed.19,20 Sjögren’s is nine times more common in women than men.5
